rubric.point: Labelled energy band diagram of an intrinsic semiconductor (E<sub>C</sub>, E<sub>V</sub>, E<sub>g</sub>, E<sub>F</sub> at mid-gap) and thermal generation of electron-hole pairs at 300 K
Definition of intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors with examples; n = p = n<sub>i</sub> for intrinsic
Donor (pentavalent, N-type) and acceptor (trivalent, P-type) impurities explained with examples and band diagrams
Energy band diagrams of conductor, semiconductor and insulator with typical E<sub>g</sub> values
Definitions: drift current, diffusion current, mobility, Fermi level, forbidden gap (with expressions)

answer: Energy bands. In a solid the discrete atomic levels broaden into bands. The highest filled band is the valence band (VB, top edge EV), the next empty band is the conduction band (CB, bottom edge EC) and the region between them is the forbidden energy gap Eg = EC − EV.

Free electrons and holes in an intrinsic semiconductor at 300 K. At 0 K the VB of pure Si/Ge is completely full and the CB completely empty, so it behaves as an insulator. At 300 K thermal energy (kT ≈ 0.026 eV) breaks some covalent bonds: an electron gains energy ≥ Eg, jumps from VB to CB and becomes a free electron, leaving behind a vacancy in the VB called a hole (an effective positive charge carrier). Electrons and holes are generated in pairs, so n = p = ni. The Fermi level EF lies near the middle of the gap. (Si: Eg = 1.1 eV, ni ≈ 1.5 × 1010 cm−3; Ge: Eg = 0.67 eV, ni ≈ 2.5 × 1013 cm−3.)

Intrinsic semiconductor: a chemically pure semiconductor with no impurity, whose carriers come only from thermal generation (n = p = ni). Extrinsic semiconductor: a semiconductor doped with a controlled amount of impurity (about 1 atom in 106–108) to raise its conductivity; n ≠ p.

Donor impurity (N-type): pentavalent atoms (P, As, Sb) substituted in Si. Four electrons form bonds and the fifth is loosely bound; it needs only ≈ 0.05 eV to enter the CB. The donor level lies just below EC; majority carriers are electrons, EF moves towards EC.

Acceptor impurity (P-type): trivalent atoms (B, Al, Ga, In) leave one bond incomplete, which accepts an electron from the VB and creates a hole. The acceptor level lies just above EV; majority carriers are holes, EF moves towards EV.

Conductor, semiconductor, insulator. Conductor: VB and CB overlap (Eg = 0), plenty of free electrons (Cu, Al). Semiconductor: small gap, Eg ≈ 1 eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.67 eV), conductivity rises with temperature. Insulator: large gap Eg > 5 eV (diamond ≈ 6 eV), CB empty and no conduction at ordinary temperature.
Drift current: current due to motion of carriers under an applied electric field E; Jdrift = q(nμn + pμp)E = σE.
Diffusion current: current due to motion of carriers from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration; Jn = qDn(dn/dx), Jp = −qDp(dp/dx), with D/μ = VT (Einstein relation).
Mobility (μ): drift velocity per unit electric field, μ = vd/E (m2/V·s or cm2/V·s); for Si μn ≈ 1300, μp ≈ 500 cm2/V·s.

Fermi level: the energy level at which the probability of occupation by an electron is exactly ½ (at T > 0); it is the reference level of the Fermi-Dirac function f(E) = 1/[1 + e(E−EF)/kT]. Forbidden energy gap: the energy range Eg between EV and EC in which no allowed electron states exist; it is the minimum energy needed to create an electron-hole pair.

rubric.point: Statement of the law of mass action: np = n<sub>i</sub>² at thermal equilibrium
Equation for N-type: n<sub>n</sub>p<sub>n</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>², with p<sub>n</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>²/N<sub>D</sub>
Equation for P-type: p<sub>p</sub>n<sub>p</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>², with n<sub>p</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>²/N<sub>A</sub>
Physical significance (recombination, product constant, minority carriers fall as doping rises)

answer: Statement. Under thermal equilibrium, at a given temperature, the product of the free electron concentration n and the hole concentration p in a semiconductor is constant and equals the square of the intrinsic concentration, irrespective of the doping: np = ni².

Reasoning. Electron-hole pairs are generated thermally at a rate g that depends only on temperature, and recombine at a rate proportional to np. At equilibrium generation = recombination, so np = constant = ni². For intrinsic material n = p = ni.
N-type. Majority electrons nn ≈ ND (donor concentration). Minority holes: pn = ni²/nn ≈ ni²/ND. So nnpn = ni².
P-type. Majority holes pp ≈ NA (acceptor concentration). Minority electrons: np = ni²/pp ≈ ni²/NA. So ppnp = ni².

Significance. Adding donors increases n; the extra electrons recombine with holes so p falls such that the product stays ni². Hence doping raises majority carriers by many orders and automatically reduces minority carriers by the same factor (e.g. Si with ND = 1016 cm−3 gives p ≈ 2.25 × 104 cm−3). The law lets us find minority carrier density from the doping and underlies the study of junction diodes and transistors. It holds only at equilibrium and for non-degenerate doping.

rubric.point: Circuit diagram for forward bias and reverse bias of a P-N diode (correct polarity of battery, series resistor, meters)

answer: P-N junction. A P-N diode has a depletion region at the junction with built-in barrier potential V0 (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge). Its behaviour with external bias V is described by the diode equation I = I0(eV/ηVT − 1).

Forward bias circuit: P side connected to the positive terminal of a variable source through a series resistor (to limit current) and a milliammeter; a voltmeter across the diode. Reverse bias circuit: the battery polarity reversed and a microammeter used.

Forward bias. The applied voltage opposes V0, so the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls to (V0 − V). For V below the cut-in (knee) voltage the current is negligible; beyond it (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge) majority carriers cross the junction in large numbers and the current rises almost exponentially. The diode is ON with a small resistance.

Reverse bias. The applied voltage aids V0; the depletion region widens and majority carriers are prevented from crossing. Only thermally generated minority carriers flow, giving a tiny, nearly constant reverse saturation current I0 (nA for Si, μA for Ge) that doubles for every 10 °C rise. The diode is OFF with very high resistance. At a sufficiently large reverse voltage (breakdown voltage VBR) the current rises sharply by avalanche/Zener breakdown.

Characteristics. The V-I curve has the forward branch in the first quadrant (zero current up to the knee, then a steep rise) and the reverse branch in the third quadrant (flat I0 then a sharp fall at VBR). This asymmetry makes the diode a one-way (rectifying) device.

Static (DC) resistance: the ratio of the DC voltage across the diode to the DC current through it at the operating point Q: Rdc = V/I. It varies with the point and is large at low current, small at high current.

Dynamic (AC) resistance: the reciprocal of the slope of the V-I curve at the operating point for small signal variation: rac = ΔV/ΔI = dV/dI = ηVT/I (≈ 26 mV/I for η = 1 at 300 K). For example at I = 2.6 mA, rac ≈ 10 Ω. In reverse bias rac is very large (MΩ), in forward bias it is of the order of a few ohms to tens of ohms.

answer: LED construction. A light emitting diode is a P-N junction made of a direct-bandgap compound semiconductor such as GaAs, GaAsP or GaP (Si and Ge are indirect-gap and do not emit light efficiently). The junction is built with a thin P layer on top, so light can escape through a transparent epoxy dome, and metal contacts are attached.

LED working. When forward biased, electrons from the N side and holes from the P side are injected across the junction and recombine near it. Each recombination releases energy approximately equal to Eg as a photon: hν = Eg, so λ(μm) = 1.24/Eg(eV). Different materials give different colours (GaAs infrared, GaAsP red/yellow, GaP green). Forward drop is about 1.6–3.4 V; a series resistor R = (VS − VF)/IF limits current to about 10–20 mA.

Tunnel diode – principle. It is a P-N junction with very heavy doping (about 1019–1020 cm−3) so that the depletion region is extremely thin (≈ 10 nm). Electrons can then tunnel through the barrier instead of climbing over it, and the degenerate bands overlap (EF lies inside the CB on the N side and inside the VB on the P side). It is made of Ge or GaAs.

Tunnel diode – V-I characteristic. At zero bias there is no net current. As forward voltage increases, the filled N-side states face empty P-side states and the tunnelling current rises to a peak (IP, VP). Increasing the voltage further shifts the bands out of alignment and the current falls to a valley (IV, VV) – this is the negative resistance region. Beyond VV the normal diffusion current of a conventional diode flows. In reverse bias it conducts heavily (like a Zener with zero breakdown voltage). Uses: high-frequency (GHz) oscillators, amplifiers, microwave switching and fast logic.

Schottky diode – construction. It is formed by a metal (Al, Au, Pt) in contact with a lightly doped N-type semiconductor (usually Si or GaAs). The junction gives a rectifying barrier (Schottky barrier). The symbol is the diode symbol with a bent bar on the cathode.

Schottky diode – working. Electrons from the semiconductor flow into the metal when forward biased; the metal side has no holes. So conduction is entirely by majority carriers and there is no minority carrier storage, hence no reverse recovery delay. The forward turn-on voltage is low (≈ 0.2–0.3 V compared with 0.7 V for Si P-N) and the junction capacitance is very small.

Schottky V-I characteristic. It resembles that of a P-N diode but with a lower knee (≈ 0.25 V), higher forward current for the same voltage, and a somewhat higher reverse leakage and lower breakdown voltage (usually below 100 V). Uses: high-speed switching (ns), SMPS and power rectifiers in low-voltage supplies, clamping in TTL gates, RF mixers and detectors.

answer: Part (a) – Given: ND = 1017 cm-3 (phosphorus, a donor), ni = 1.5 × 1010 cm-3, μn = 1300, μp = 500 cm2/V·s, q = 1.6 × 10-19 C.
Since ND ≫ ni, majority (electron) concentration n ≈ ND = 1017 cm-3.
Minority (hole) concentration from the law of mass action: p = ni²/n = (1.5 × 1010)²/1017 = 2.25 × 1020/1017 = 2.25 × 103 cm-3.
Conductivity σ = q(nμn + pμp) = 1.6 × 10-19 × (1017 × 1300 + 2.25 × 103 × 500) = 1.6 × 10-19 × (1.3 × 1020 + 1.1 × 106) ≈ 20.8 S/cm (hole term is negligible).
Part (b) – (i) Intrinsic Si: n = p = ni. σi = qni(μn + μp) = 1.6 × 10-19 × 1.5 × 1010 × (1300 + 500) = 1.6 × 10-19 × 1.5 × 1010 × 1800 = 4.32 × 10-6 S/cm.
(ii) Donor 1 in 108 atoms: ND = 5 × 1022/108 = 5 × 1014 cm-3 ≫ ni, so n ≈ 5 × 1014, p = 2.25 × 1020/5 × 1014 = 4.5 × 105 cm-3. σ ≈ qnμn = 1.6 × 10-19 × 5 × 1014 × 1300 = 0.104 S/cm.
(iii) Acceptor 1 in 5 × 107 atoms: NA = 5 × 1022/5 × 107 = 1015 cm-3, so p ≈ 1015, n = 2.25 × 1020/1015 = 2.25 × 105 cm-3. σ ≈ qpμp = 1.6 × 10-19 × 1015 × 500 = 0.08 S/cm.
Conclusion: a doping of only 1 part in 108 raises the conductivity of silicon by a factor of about 2.4 × 104.

answer: Energy bands in materials. Atomic energy levels merge into the valence band (VB) and conduction band (CB), separated by the forbidden gap Eg. Conductor: VB and CB overlap (no gap). Semiconductor: small gap, about 0.7–1.5 eV (Ge 0.67 eV, Si 1.1 eV, GaAs 1.4 eV). Insulator: large gap above 5 eV. In a semiconductor electrons jump from VB to CB on thermal or optical excitation, leaving holes in the VB.
LED principle. In a forward biased P-N junction of a direct-gap semiconductor, electrons in the CB recombine with holes in the VB and the released energy is emitted as a photon: E = hν = hc/λ = Eg.
Given: Eg = 1.875 eV, h = 6.6 × 10-34 J·s, c = 3 × 108 m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10-19 J.
This wavelength lies between about 620 and 700 nm, so the emitted light is red, which is what GaAsP LEDs are known for.

answer: (a) Full-wave bridge rectifier. Circuit: the secondary of the transformer (vs = Vm sin ωt) is connected across two opposite corners of a bridge of four diodes D1–D4; the load RL is connected across the other two corners.

Working. Positive half-cycle: the upper end of the secondary is positive, D1 and D3 are forward biased (D2, D4 reverse biased); current flows through RL from top to bottom. Negative half-cycle: D2 and D4 conduct (D1, D3 off) and the current again flows through RL in the same direction. Hence the load voltage is a pulsating dc consisting of both half-cycles, with frequency 2f.
Derivation of η (ideal diodes, forward resistance rf neglected for the maximum value). Let i = Im sin ωt, Im = Vm/(RL + 2rf).
Step 1: I<sub>dc</sub> = (1/π)∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> I<sub>m</sub> sin θ dθ = 2I<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.636 I<sub>m</sub>.
Step 2: I<sub>rms</sub> = √[(1/π)∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> I<sub>m</sub>² sin²θ dθ] = I<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 I<sub>m</sub>.
Step 3: dc output power P<sub>dc</sub> = I<sub>dc</sub>² R<sub>L</sub> = (4I<sub>m</sub>²/π²) R<sub>L</sub>.
Step 4: ac input power P<sub>ac</sub> = I<sub>rms</sub>²(R<sub>L</sub> + 2r<sub>f</sub>) = (I<sub>m</sub>²/2)(R<sub>L</sub> + 2r<sub>f</sub>).
Step 5: η = Pdc/Pac = (8/π²)·RL/(RL + 2rf) = 0.811/(1 + 2rf/RL). For rf << RL: ηmax = 8/π² = 81.2 %. Other figures: γ = 0.482, PIV = Vm, TUF = 0.812 (no dc saturation of transformer).

(b) Full-wave centre-tap rectifier. A transformer with centre-tapped secondary gives two equal voltages Vm sin ωt, 180° out of phase, to D1 and D2; the load RL is connected between the centre-tap and the joined cathodes. In the positive half-cycle D1 conducts (D2 off); in the negative half-cycle D2 conducts (D1 off). The load current iL always flows in one direction, giving |sin ωt| across RL. PIV of each diode = 2Vm.

Efficiency. η = Pdc/Pac = (4Im²RL/π²)/[(Im²/2)(RL + rf)] = 8/π² × RL/(RL+rf) → 81.2 % (ideal diodes), twice that of a half-wave rectifier (40.6 %). The ripple factor (0.482) is lower than that of a half-wave rectifier (1.21).

Avalanche breakdown mechanism: carrier multiplication by impact ionisation in a wide depletion region, V<sub>B</sub> > 6 V

Comparison on doping and depletion width
Comparison on electric field and temperature coefficient (positive vs negative)

answer: Breakdown. When the reverse bias on a P-N junction is raised beyond a critical value (the breakdown voltage VBR), the reverse current rises abruptly while the voltage across the diode remains almost constant. If the current is limited externally, the junction is not damaged; two mechanisms are responsible.

1. Avalanche breakdown. Occurs in lightly doped junctions with a wide depletion region (VB usually > 6 V). Minority carriers crossing the depletion region gain kinetic energy from the field; when the energy is sufficient they collide with lattice atoms and knock out covalent-bond electrons (impact ionisation), producing new electron-hole pairs. These are accelerated and ionise more atoms; the multiplication (M = 1/[1 − (V/VB)n]) becomes infinite at V = VB and a large reverse current flows.

2. Zener breakdown. Occurs in heavily doped junctions having a very narrow depletion region (VZ < 5–6 V). Even a small reverse voltage produces a very high field (≈ 106 V/cm) across the narrow region, which directly pulls electrons out of covalent bonds (field ionisation / tunnelling). The free carriers produce a sudden large reverse current at a sharp, well-defined voltage.
Comparison:
Doping: avalanche – light/moderate; Zener – heavy.
Depletion width: avalanche – wide; Zener – very narrow.
Electric field intensity: avalanche – relatively lower field but long path for carriers to gain energy; Zener – very high field (> 2 × 107 V/m) at low voltage.
Mechanism: avalanche – impact ionisation and carrier multiplication; Zener – field (tunnelling) emission.

Temperature coefficient: avalanche – positive (VB increases with T because lattice vibration shortens the mean free path); Zener – negative (VZ decreases with T because thermal energy helps in breaking bonds). At about 5–6 V both effects cancel (zero temperature coefficient).
V-I characteristic: avalanche – gradual rounded knee; Zener – very sharp knee with nearly vertical characteristic.
Use: avalanche – avalanche photodiodes, surge protection; Zener – voltage reference and regulator.

answer: Clipper. A circuit that removes (clips) the part of the input waveform above or below a chosen reference level without distorting the remaining part. It uses diodes, resistors and (optionally) dc batteries but no energy-storing element.

Classification: (i) series clipper – diode in series with the load; (ii) shunt (parallel) clipper – diode in parallel with the load; each can be positive (clips +ve peaks), negative (clips −ve peaks), biased (with reference VR) or combinational/two-level (two diodes and two batteries clipping both peaks).

Positive shunt clipper (ideal diode). Series R, diode D connected across the output with its cathode to the reference VR (anode to the output). For vi < VR D is off, vo = vi. For vi > VR D conducts and vo = VR (+0.7 V for a Si diode). Positive peaks above VR are removed. Reversing the diode (and battery) clips the negative peaks.
Transfer characteristic: a straight line of slope 1 up to vi = VR, then horizontal at vo = VR.

Clamper. A circuit that adds a dc level to the input ac signal, shifting the whole waveform up or down without changing its shape. It uses a capacitor, a diode and a resistor (and a battery for biased clamping) with the time-constant condition RC >> T (usually 5RC > 10 T) so that the capacitor does not discharge appreciably during the off-period of the diode.

Biased positive clamper. Circuit: input vi → series capacitor C → output node; diode D connected from the output node to ground with its cathode at the output node and anode through a battery VR (anode side reference), RL across the output. (For a positive clamp the diode is oriented so that it conducts on the negative peak.)

Operation (ideal diode), input square/sine wave of peak Vm: During the first negative peak, D is forward biased and C charges to VC = Vm + VR with the output-side plate positive, so the output is held at VR at the negative peak. When vi rises the diode turns off; since τ = RC is large, C retains its voltage and acts as a battery in series with the input.

Steady state: vo = vi + Vm + VR. The negative peak (−Vm) is lifted to +VR and the positive peak becomes 2Vm + VR: the waveform is clamped to the positive side at level VR, with total swing 2Vm unchanged. Using a Si diode the clamped level shifts by −0.7 V.
Applications: restoring the dc component in TV receivers, voltage doublers/multipliers, test equipment.

answer: Principle. A voltage multiplier uses diodes as switches and capacitors as storage elements to produce a dc output equal to an integral multiple of the peak input voltage Vm (without a high-voltage transformer). A tripler gives Vdc ≈ 3Vm.

Circuit. An ac source vi = Vm sin ωt feeds capacitor C1 in series; D1 connects the C1-diode node to ground (clamping), D2 connects that node to C2 (top plate of the second stage), D3 passes charge on to C3; C2 returns to the ac source side. The load RL is connected across the series combination of C1 and C3.
Step 1 (first negative half-cycle): D1 conducts and C1 charges to Vm (it acts as a clamper).
Step 2 (positive half-cycle): D1 off; source (Vm) in series with C1 (Vm) = 2Vm forward biases D2 and charges C2 to 2Vm.

Step 3 (next negative half-cycle): D2 off, D3 conducts; C2 (2Vm) is in series with the source and C1 in such a way that the net charging voltage of C3 is VC2 + Vm − VC1 = 2Vm + Vm − Vm = 2Vm, so C3 charges to 2Vm.

Output: vo = VC1 + VC3 = Vm + 2Vm = 3Vm. In the same circuit the voltage across C2 alone is 2Vm (doubler output); one more diode-capacitor stage gives a quadrupler (4Vm). The PIV of each diode is 2Vm.

Notes: output reaches 3Vm after a few cycles, regulation is poor (voltage falls rapidly with load current), so tripler circuits are used for high-voltage, low-current applications such as CRT anodes, photocopiers and ion pumps.

rubric.point: Zener V-I characteristic and its constant-voltage property in breakdown region
Circuit diagram of shunt regulator: R<sub>s</sub>, reverse-biased Zener across R<sub>L</sub>
Line regulation: V<sub>in</sub> change absorbed by R<sub>s</sub> and I<sub>Z</sub>, V<sub>L</sub> constant
Load regulation: change in R<sub>L</sub> compensated by I<sub>Z</sub> (I<sub>S</sub> = I<sub>Z</sub> + I<sub>L</sub> constant)
Conditions for regulation (I<sub>ZK</sub> ≤ I<sub>Z</sub> ≤ I<sub>ZM</sub>) and design equations

answer: Zener characteristic. In reverse breakdown a Zener diode maintains an almost constant voltage VZ across its terminals while the current varies widely between IZ,min (knee current IZK) and IZ,max (IZM, set by the power rating PZ = VZIZM). The small slope is the dynamic resistance rz (a few ohms).

Circuit. The unregulated supply Vin is connected through a series resistor Rs to the Zener diode (cathode toward the positive side) and the load RL is connected in parallel with the Zener. Output VL = VZ. Currents: IS = (Vin − VZ)/Rs = IZ + IL, where IL = VZ/RL.

Line regulation (Vin varies, RL fixed). If Vin increases, IS increases. Since VL = VZ is constant, IL is constant, so the whole extra current ΔIS = ΔVin/Rs is taken by the Zener (IZ rises). The extra voltage drops across Rs (VR = Vin − VZ) and the output stays at VZ. When Vin decreases, IZ decreases, and again VL ≈ VZ as long as IZ ≥ IZK.

Load regulation (RL varies, Vin fixed). IS = (Vin − VZ)/Rs is constant. If RL decreases, IL increases and the Zener current falls by the same amount (IZ = IS − IL); if RL increases, IZ rises. The drop in Rs and VL remain unchanged. The Zener thus acts as a variable shunt that diverts the surplus current.

Conditions for good regulation: (i) Vin > VZ; (ii) IZ must stay between IZK and IZM. Hence Rs,min = (Vin,max − VZ)/(IZM + IL,min) and Rs,max = (Vin,min − VZ)/(IZK + IL,max). Minimum RL for regulation: RL,min = VZRs/(Vin,min − VZ).
Practical measures: line regulation = ΔVL/ΔVin ≈ rz/(Rs + rz), load regulation = −(Rs ∥ rz) ≈ −rz. Used in low-power regulated supplies and reference sources.

answer: Assumed circuit: input vi(t) = 5 sin(100πt) V applied through series R; across the output is a diode D (anode to output node) in series with a 1 V battery whose positive terminal faces the cathode, i.e. D conducts when vi > 1 V (positive shunt clipper at 1 V). Diode treated as ideal.
Signal data: Vm = 5 V, ω = 100π rad/s → f = 50 Hz, T = 20 ms.
Case 1: vi < 1 V (including the whole negative half-cycle) – D is reverse biased (open). No current flows through R, so vo = vi.
Case 2: vi ≥ 1 V – D conducts and acts as a short circuit in series with the 1 V battery; vo = 1 V, and the excess vi − 1 appears across R.
Transfer characteristic (vo vs vi): vo = vi for −5 V ≤ vi ≤ 1 V (45° line through the origin) and vo = 1 V (horizontal line) for 1 V ≤ vi ≤ 5 V; the break point is at (1 V, 1 V).
Clipping instants: 5 sin(100πt) = 1 → sin θ = 0.2 → θ1 = 11.54° (0.2014 rad). t1 = θ/ω = 0.2014/(100π) = 0.641 ms; second crossing at θ2 = 180° − 11.54° = 168.46°, t2 = 9.359 ms.

Output waveform: 0 → 0.641 ms follows the sine up to 1 V; 0.641 → 9.359 ms flat at +1 V; 9.359 → 10 ms follows the sine down to 0; during 10–20 ms the negative half-cycle is reproduced unchanged down to −5 V. For a Si diode (Vγ = 0.7 V) the flat level would be 1.7 V.
Conclusion: the circuit is a positive peak clipper with clipping level +1 V; peak-to-peak output = 6 V.

answer: Assumed network: series capacitor C = 1 μF, load RL = 100 kΩ across the output, and a diode in parallel with the output in series with a 1.5 V battery, oriented so that the diode conducts when the output falls below +1.5 V (cathode at the output node, anode at the +1.5 V battery terminal). Ideal diode; input square wave of ±20 V at 1 kHz.
(i) Time constant: τ = RLC = 100 × 103 × 1 × 10-6 = 0.1 s. Hence 5τ = 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 s = 500 ms.

(ii) Comparison: T = 1/f = 1/1000 = 1 ms, so T/2 = 0.5 ms. 5τ/(T/2) = 500 ms/0.5 ms = 1000, i.e. 5τ >> T/2. The capacitor cannot discharge appreciably through RL during the half-period when the diode is off, so the circuit behaves as a proper clamper (the output is the input shifted by a constant dc level).

(iii) Steady state. During the first −20 V half-cycle the diode conducts and the capacitor charges rapidly (through the diode, with small resistance) until the output is at the battery voltage: vo = +1.5 V. KVL around the input loop with vo = vi + VC (VC positive on the output side): 1.5 = −20 + VC, so VC = 20 + 1.5 = 21.5 V.
When the input switches to +20 V, the diode turns off (v<sub>o</sub> > 1.5 V) and the capacitor holds 21.5 V: v<sub>o</sub> = 20 + 21.5 = 41.5 V.

Output waveform: square wave vo = vi + 21.5 V swinging between +1.5 V (during the −20 V half) and +41.5 V (during the +20 V half); the peak-to-peak swing, 40 V, equals the input swing, the waveform being clamped (shifted up) so that its negative extreme sits at the +1.5 V reference. The slight droop in each half-cycle is negligible because 5τ >> T/2 (droop ≈ 0.5 ms/100 ms of 40 V ≈ 0.2 V).
Conclusion: positive-going clamper with level shift of +21.5 V.
Q2.7.result: 5τ = 0.5 s (500 ms); T/2 = 0.5 ms, so 5τ = 1000 × (T/2); output square wave between +1.5 V and +41.5 V (shift +21.5 V). (Assumed diode orientation: clamps negative peak to +1.5 V.)

answer: (a) Remove the Zener: VL = VinRL/(Rs + RL) = 16 × 3/(1 + 3) = 12 V > VZ = 10 V, so the Zener is ON (in breakdown).
VL = VZ = 10 V. VR = 16 − 10 = 6 V. IR = 6 V/1 kΩ = 6 mA. IL = 10/3 kΩ = 3.33 mA. IZ = IR − IL = 6 − 3.33 = 2.67 mA. PZ = VZIZ = 10 × 2.67 mA = 26.7 mW.
(b) Load current IL = VZ/RL = 20/1.2 kΩ = 16.67 mA (constant while Zener ON).
Minimum Vi (Zener just on, IZ = 0): VL = 20 V = ViRL/(R + RL) → Vi,min = 20 × (220 + 1200)/1200 = 23.67 V.
Maximum Vi (IZ = IZM = 60 mA): IR,max = IZM + IL = 60 + 16.67 = 76.67 mA; Vi,max = VZ + IR,maxR = 20 + 76.67 mA × 220 = 20 + 16.87 = 36.87 V. Range: 23.67 V ≤ Vi ≤ 36.87 V.

(c) The Zener (VZ = VL = 12 V) must supply the load up to 200 mA at fixed Vin = 16 V. Series current is constant, IS = (16 − 12)/Rs. To supply the full 200 mA at maximum load (Zener current taken as ≈ 0, ideal knee) IS ≥ 200 mA → Rs = 4 V/200 mA = 20 Ω (in practice a little less to keep IZK flowing).
At no load (IL = 0) the Zener carries the full 200 mA: PZ,max = 12 × 0.2 = 2.4 W, so choose a 12 V, 3 W Zener (and Rs power rating I²R = 0.04 × 20 = 0.8 W → 1 W).

(d) With the Zener ON at 6 V: IR = (12 − 6)/500 = 12 mA (constant). The Zener must keep at least IZK = 5 mA, so the load can take IL,max = 12 − 5 = 7 mA. RL,min = VZ/IL,max = 6/7 mA = 857 Ω (857 Ω or more keeps output ≥ 6 V).

rubric.point: (a) Construction diagram of NPN/PNP BJT (emitter heavily doped, base thin and lightly doped, collector large) with biasing
(a) Internal current components: I<sub>En</sub>, I<sub>Ep</sub>, recombination current, I<sub>Cn</sub>, I<sub>CBO</sub>; I<sub>E</sub> = I<sub>B</sub> + I<sub>C</sub>
(b) Definitions of α, β, γ with expressions
(b) Derivation β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(1 + β)
(b) Other relation: I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub> + (1 + β)I<sub>CBO</sub> and γ = 1/(1 − α) = 1 + β
(c) Comparison BJT vs FET (at least 4 points)

answer: (a) Construction. A BJT is a three-layer, two-junction device (NPN or PNP). Emitter: heavily doped, emits carriers; base: very thin (≈ 1 μm) and lightly doped; collector: moderately doped and largest in area, collects carriers. In the active region the emitter-base junction (JE) is forward biased and the collector-base junction (JC) is reverse biased.

Current components (NPN). (1) Forward bias of JE makes electrons from the emitter flow into the base (IEn) and holes flow from base to emitter (IEp – small because of low base doping); IE = IEn + IEp. (2) A very small fraction (≈ 1–5 %) of the injected electrons recombines with holes in the base, forming the base recombination current. (3) The remaining electrons, being minority carriers in the base, diffuse across the thin base and are swept by the collector field into the collector (ICn). (4) In addition the reverse-biased JC carries a small reverse saturation current ICBO of thermally generated minority carriers. Hence IC = αIE + ICBO; IB = IE − IC = (1 − α)IE − ICBO and IE = IB + IC. In a PNP transistor the roles of electrons and holes are interchanged and all currents reverse in direction.
(b) Definitions. αdc = IC/IE (CB current gain, 0.95–0.995); βdc = IC/IB (CE current gain, 20–500); γ = IE/IB (CC current gain).
Derivation. Step 1: IE = IB + IC.
Step 2: divide by I<sub>C</sub>: I<sub>E</sub>/I<sub>C</sub> = I<sub>B</sub>/I<sub>C</sub> + 1 → 1/α = 1/β + 1.

Step 5: γ = I<sub>E</sub>/I<sub>B</sub> = (I<sub>B</sub> + I<sub>C</sub>)/I<sub>B</sub> = 1 + β = 1/(1 − α). Also I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub> + (1 + β)I<sub>CBO</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub> + I<sub>CEO</sub>. (Example: α = 0.98 → β = 49.)

(c) BJT vs FET: (1) BJT is a current-controlled device; FET is voltage-controlled. (2) BJT is bipolar (both electrons and holes carry current); FET is unipolar (majority carriers only). (3) Input resistance: BJT low (≈ 1 kΩ); FET very high (107–1012 Ω). (4) Noise: BJT higher; FET lower. (5) Thermal stability: BJT has thermal runaway (negative-feedback needed); FET has negative temperature coefficient of current, thermally stable. (6) Size: FET occupies less area, ideal for ICs; (7) Gain-bandwidth: BJT has higher voltage gain; FET has lower. (8) Switching speed/power: MOSFET has lower power consumption in digital circuits. (9) FET is more susceptible to static damage (MOSFET gate).

answer: (a) CE configuration. The emitter is common to input (base-emitter) and output (collector-emitter). For an NPN transistor: VBB (variable) in series with RB forward-biases the base-emitter junction (+ at base) and VCC (variable) makes the collector positive with respect to emitter. A μA meter measures IB, an mA meter measures IC.

Input characteristic: IB vs VBE for constant VCE. The curve resembles the forward characteristic of a diode: negligible current up to cut-in voltage (≈ 0.5 V Si) then an exponential rise. Increasing VCE shifts the curve slightly to the right (reduced base width, Early effect, smaller IB). Input resistance ri = ΔVBE/ΔIB at constant VCE (≈ 1 kΩ).

Output characteristics: IC vs VCE for different constant IB. For VCE above a small knee value (≈ 0.2 V) IC rises slowly and almost flat with VCE (slight upward slope due to base-width modulation); higher IB gives a higher curve with IC = βIB. Output resistance ro = ΔVCE/ΔIC at constant IB (≈ 40 kΩ); βac = ΔIC/ΔIB at constant VCE.

Regions: Active – JE forward, JC reverse biased (VCE > VCE(sat)); used for amplification. Saturation – both junctions forward biased, VCE ≈ 0.2 V (left of the knee), IC maximum, switch ON. Cut-off – both junctions reverse biased (IB = 0), only ICEO flows; switch OFF.

(b) CB configuration. Base is common. For an NPN: emitter supply VEE makes the emitter negative with respect to the base (forward bias); VCC makes the collector positive with respect to the base (reverse bias). (For PNP all polarities are reversed.) Input current IE, output current IC.

Input characteristic: IE vs VEB at constant VCB – diode-like curve with cut-in 0.5 V; with higher VCB the curve shifts left (more IE for a given VEB) because of reduced base width. Input resistance is very low (20–100 Ω).

Output characteristics: IC vs VCB at constant IE. Active region: JE forward, JC reverse; IC ≈ αIE nearly constant (curves almost horizontal; ro very high, ≈ 1 MΩ). Saturation: JC forward biased (VCB slightly negative) and IC falls rapidly to zero. Cut-off: IE = 0, IC = ICBO. Current gain α = ΔIC/ΔIE (just less than 1), so CB gives voltage gain but no current gain.

answer: (a) Biasing is the process of applying suitable dc voltages and currents so that the transistor operates at a fixed quiescent point (Q-point: ICQ, VCEQ) in the active region, in the middle of the load line, so that the ac signal is amplified without distortion.

Requirements: (i) Q-point must lie in the active region and give maximum undistorted swing; (ii) the Q-point must remain stable (independent of transistor replacement and temperature); (iii) simple, economical circuit with few components; (iv) low power dissipation and no thermal runaway.

Need for stabilisation. IC = βIB + (1 + β)ICBO. ICBO doubles every 10 °C, VBE falls by ≈ 2.5 mV/°C and β varies from unit to unit (and with T and IC). Without stabilisation these shift the Q-point into saturation/cut-off and may cause thermal runaway (rise of IC → more heat → more ICBO). Stability factor S = ∂IC/∂ICBO; ideally S = 1.
(b) Fixed bias. VCC feeds the base through RB and the collector through RC. KVL for the base loop: VCC − IBRB − VBE = 0.
I<sub>BQ</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/R<sub>B</sub> (≈ V<sub>CC</sub>/R<sub>B</sub> for Si, V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V).
I<sub>CQ</sub> = βI<sub>BQ</sub> (+ (1 + β)I<sub>CBO</sub>); collector loop: V<sub>CEQ</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>CQ</sub>R<sub>C</sub>.

Disadvantages: (i) ICQ depends directly on β, so the Q-point shifts when β changes with the transistor or temperature; (ii) stability factor S = 1 + β is very high (≈ 100), so poor thermal stability and possible thermal runaway; (iii) no feedback to correct drift. Used only where stability is not critical (switching).

(c) Voltage-divider (potential-divider) bias. R1 and R2 form a divider across VCC giving the base voltage; RC in the collector, RE (with bypass CE) in the emitter. Thevenin equivalent of the base network: VTH = VCCR2/(R1 + R2), RTH = R1∥R2.
Base loop: VTH = IBRTH + VBE + IERE, with IE = (1 + β)IB → IB = (VTH − VBE)/(RTH + (1 + β)RE); IC = βIB; collector loop: VCE = VCC − ICRC − IERE ≈ VCC − IC(RC + RE).

Why most stable. If RTH << (1 + β)RE (design rule R2 ≈ 10RE), IE ≈ (VTH − VBE)/RE, independent of β. Stability factor S = (1 + β)(1 + RTH/RE)/(1 + β + RTH/RE) ≈ 1 + RTH/RE (≈ 5–10, close to ideal 1). Negative feedback through RE: any increase in IC raises IERE, reduces VBE and IB, restoring IC. Hence the Q-point is nearly independent of β, T and ICBO.
formulas: Fixed bias: I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/R<sub>B</sub>; I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub>; V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>R<sub>C</sub>; S = 1 + β

answer: Low-frequency h-parameter model (CE). Hybrid equations: Vbe = hieIb + hreVce; Ic = hfeIb + hoeVce. Equivalent circuit: input loop has source VS with RS, hie and a voltage source hreVce; output has a current source hfeIb in parallel with 1/hoe and the load RL. IL = −Ic.

(i) Current gain. The load current IL flows out of the collector into RL, so IL = −Ic and Vce = ILRL = −IcRL. From Ic = hfeIb + hoeVce = hfeIb − hoeRLIc we get Ic(1 + hoeRL) = hfeIb. Hence Ai = IL/Ib = −hfe/(1 + hoeRL) (≈ −hfe when hoeRL << 1).
(ii) Input resistance. Ri = Vbe/Ib = hie + hreVce/Ib. Using Vce = ILRL = AiIbRL: Ri = hie + hreAiRL = hie − hfehreRL/(1 + hoeRL) (≈ hie).
(iii) Voltage gain. Av = Vo/Vi = (ILRL)/(IbRi) → Av = AiRL/Ri = −hfeRL/[hie + (hiehoe − hfehre)RL], negative (180° phase shift) and large (≈ −hfeRL/hie).

(iv) Output resistance. Set VS = 0, remove RL and apply Vce. Input loop: Ib = −hreVce/(hie + RS). Then Ic = hfeIb + hoeVce = Vce[hoe − hfehre/(hie + RS)], so Ro = Vce/Ic = 1/[hoe − hfehre/(hie + RS)], high (≈ 40–80 kΩ).
re model (CE, voltage-divider biased). The base-emitter junction is replaced by βre, with re = 26 mV/IE, and a collector current source βIb in parallel with ro.

Input impedance: Zi = RB∥βre (with emitter bypassed), ≈ βre if RB >> βre. Output impedance: Zo = RC∥ro ≈ RC (ro >> RC). Voltage gain: Vo = −βIb(RC∥ro∥RL) and Vi = Ibβre, so Av = −(RC∥ro∥RL)/re ≈ −RC/re (unloaded). Current gain: Ai = Io/Ii = β (neglecting RB and ro); in general Ai = −AvZi/RL.

answer: (a) Construction. An n-channel JFET consists of an n-type silicon bar with ohmic contacts at the two ends, source (S) and drain (D). Heavily doped p+ regions are diffused on both sides of the bar and connected together to form the gate (G). The narrow n-region between the gate junctions is the channel. Normally the gate-channel p-n junction is reverse biased (VGS ≤ 0), so the gate current is of the order of nA and the input resistance is very high (108 Ω).

Working. With VGS = 0 and small VDS, electrons flow from source to drain through the channel and the device behaves as a resistor (ID ∝ VDS). As VDS increases, the voltage drop along the channel reverse biases the gate junction more near the drain, so the depletion region is wedge shaped and narrows the channel there. At VDS = |VP| the depletion layers almost touch (pinch-off) and ID becomes nearly constant at IDSS. Making VGS more negative widens the depletion regions, reducing the channel width and ID; at VGS = VP (cut-off) ID ≈ 0. Hence ID is controlled by the gate voltage (voltage-controlled device, unipolar).
(b) Parameters. (i) Pinch-off voltage VP: the gate-source voltage at which the channel is fully depleted and ID ≈ 0 (for VGS = 0 it is the VDS at which ID saturates), e.g. −4 V.
(ii) IDSS: the maximum drain current for VGS = 0 in the saturation (pinch-off) region.
(iii) Transconductance gm = ΔID/ΔVGS at constant VDS (mS). gm = gm0(1 − VGS/VP), gm0 = 2IDSS/|VP|.
(iv) Drain (dynamic) resistance rd = ΔVDS/ΔID at constant VGS (≈ 10 kΩ–1 MΩ; large in saturation).
(v) Amplification factor μ = ΔVDS/ΔVGS at constant ID. The three are related by μ = rdgm.

(c) Drain characteristics (ID vs VDS at constant VGS). For each VGS (0, −1, −2 V …): ohmic (triode) region for small VDS where ID rises linearly (voltage-controlled resistor); saturation (pinch-off) region where ID is almost constant – the amplifier region, with VDS ≥ VGS − VP; breakdown region at large VDS where avalanche breakdown of the gate junction occurs and ID rises sharply. The top curve is VGS = 0 (IDSS); more negative VGS gives lower curves, and the cut-off curve is VGS = VP.

Transfer characteristic (ID vs VGS at constant VDS in saturation). A parabola from IDSS at VGS = 0 to zero at VGS = VP, given by the Shockley equation ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VP)². It is obtained by projecting the saturation values of the drain curves.

(b) Working in depletion mode (V<sub>GS</sub> negative) and enhancement mode (V<sub>GS</sub> positive)
(b) Characteristics (transfer curve through I<sub>DSS</sub>) and explanation for both modes

answer: (a) N-channel enhancement MOSFET (E-MOSFET). Construction: a lightly doped p-type substrate with two heavily doped n+ regions (source and drain). A thin SiO2 layer (≈ 10-8 m) covers the region between them and a metal gate is deposited on the oxide, insulating the gate from the substrate. No channel exists physically; the substrate is usually tied to the source.

Working: With VGS = 0 the two n+-p junctions are back to back, so ID ≈ 0. A positive VGS repels holes from the surface under the gate and attracts minority electrons. At a threshold voltage VT (≈ 1–3 V) a thin n-type inversion layer (induced channel) forms between source and drain. For VGS > VT, a larger VGS increases the channel conductivity (enhances it), hence the name. With VDS applied, ID flows; when VDS ≥ VGS − VT the channel pinches off at the drain end and ID saturates.

Characteristics: Drain characteristic: for VGS > VT, ohmic region (ID = k[2(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS²]) then saturation region (flat); the curves for VGS = VT, VT+1, … are equally spaced upwards. Transfer characteristic: ID = 0 until VGS = VT, then ID = k(VGS − VT)2 (parabola). It is operated only with positive gate bias (n-channel).

(b) N-channel depletion MOSFET (D-MOSFET). Construction: similar to the E-MOSFET but with an n-type channel diffused between the n+ source and drain during manufacture (a physically present channel). The gate is insulated by SiO2, so gate current is ≈ 10-12 A.

Working – depletion mode: A negative VGS repels electrons from the channel and induces positive charge in it, depleting (reducing) the carriers. ID decreases until pinch-off at VGS = VP (negative, e.g. −4 V).
Working – enhancement mode: A positive VGS attracts additional electrons into the channel, increasing its conductivity; ID exceeds IDSS.

Characteristics: The transfer characteristic is the Shockley parabola ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VP)² extended to positive VGS; it passes through IDSS at VGS = 0 and cuts the axis at VP. The drain characteristics are like those of a JFET but with curves for both negative and positive VGS.

Why both modes? Because the channel already exists at VGS = 0 and the gate is insulated by the oxide, the gate can be biased of either polarity without forward-biasing a junction (as would happen in a JFET). Negative gate voltage depletes, positive enhances the channel carriers, so the D-MOSFET can operate in both modes. Very high input resistance (1010–1015 Ω).

answer: A comparative table of BJT and FET (JFET/MOSFET) is given below (property – BJT – FET):
Controlled by: BJT – base current (current-controlled); FET – gate-source voltage (voltage-controlled).
Carriers: BJT – bipolar (electrons and holes); FET – unipolar (majority carriers only).
Input resistance: BJT – low (1–2 kΩ, forward-biased junction); FET – very high (JFET 108 Ω, MOSFET 1010–1015 Ω).
Output / gain parameters: BJT – higher voltage gain and larger gm (IC/VT); FET – lower gm (mS) and gain-bandwidth product.

Thermal stability: BJT – thermal runaway (IC rises with T); FET – negative temperature coefficient, more stable.
Size and construction: BJT – larger, complex fabrication; FET – smaller, simpler, occupies less area, preferred in VLSI.

Offset voltage: BJT has an offset voltage VCE(sat) at zero collector current; FET has none, making it a good chopper/analog switch. Handling: BJT – robust; MOSFET – the thin oxide is easily damaged by static charge. Power and speed: BJT switches faster in some cases but dissipates more power; MOSFET consumes almost no static power (CMOS).

answer: Circuit. An n-channel JFET in common-source (CS) configuration with self bias: gate returned to ground via RG (≈ 1 MΩ), source resistor RS bypassed by CS, drain resistor RD connected to VDD. The input vi is applied to the gate through coupling capacitor C1, the output vo is taken from the drain through C2 across RL.

Phase relationship. During the positive half-cycle of vi, VGS becomes less negative, ID increases, the drop IDRD increases and the drain voltage VDS = VDD − IDRD decreases. Hence the output is 180° out of phase with the input (inverting amplifier).

AC equivalent model. Short VDD and capacitors. The JFET is replaced by a voltage-controlled current source gmvgs (drain to source) in parallel with rd. The gate draws no current, so vgs = vi (source grounded through CS). The load seen by the current source is rd, RD and RL in parallel.
Derivation. Step 1: output current source: id = gmvgs (from drain to source).

Step 2: this current flows through the parallel load R' = r<sub>d</sub>∥R<sub>D</sub>∥R<sub>L</sub>, producing v<sub>o</sub> = −i<sub>d</sub>R' (the minus sign because the current flows from drain to ground, making the drain voltage fall).
Step 3: v<sub>o</sub> = −g<sub>m</sub>v<sub>i</sub>R'.
Step 4: Av = vo/vi = −gm(rd∥RD∥RL). For rd >> RD and no load, Av ≈ −gmRD; in terms of μ = gmrd: Av = −μRD/(rd + RD) (unloaded).
Impedances: Zi = RG (very high, since gate current ≈ 0); Zo = rd∥RD ≈ RD.
Remark. If CS is omitted (unbypassed RS), the gain falls to Av = −gmRD/(1 + gmRS) due to negative feedback (rd neglected). Example: gm = 3 mS, RD = 4.7 kΩ → |Av| ≈ 14.

answer: Biasing fixes the operating point (VGS, ID, VDS) of the JFET in the saturation (pinch-off) region. Since the gate current is zero, the voltage across RG is zero.

(a) Fixed (battery) bias. The gate is connected through RG (≈ 1 MΩ) to a separate negative supply VGG, the source is grounded and the drain is connected to VDD via RD. Gate loop: VGS = −VGG (IGRG = 0).

Drain current from Shockley's equation: I<sub>D</sub> = I<sub>DSS</sub>(1 − V<sub>GS</sub>/V<sub>P</sub>)²; drain loop: V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>D</sub>. Disadvantage: needs two supplies, and the Q-point varies widely with the I<sub>DSS</sub>, V<sub>P</sub> spread of devices.

(b) Self bias. A resistor RS is placed between the source and ground (often bypassed by CS) and the gate returns to ground via RG. The drain current ID through RS raises the source above ground: VS = IDRS. Since VG = 0, VGS = −IDRS, i.e. a reverse bias is generated automatically from a single supply.

Substitute in the Shockley equation: ID = IDSS(1 + IDRS/VP)² — a quadratic in ID (choose the root with |VGS| < |VP|), or find the intersection of the bias line VGS = −IDRS with the transfer curve graphically. Then VDS = VDD − ID(RD + RS).
Advantage: negative feedback through RS stabilises ID (if ID rises, VGS becomes more negative and reduces it), and only one supply is needed.

I<sub>G</sub> = 0, so the voltage drop across R<sub>G</sub> is zero and V<sub>G</sub> = 0. Gate-source loop: V<sub>GS</sub> = −I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>S</sub> = −I<sub>D</sub> (with I<sub>D</sub> in mA and R<sub>S</sub> = 1 kΩ).
Shockley equation: I<sub>D</sub> = I<sub>DSS</sub>(1 − V<sub>GS</sub>/V<sub>P</sub>)² = 10(1 − (−I<sub>D</sub>)/(−4))² = 10(1 − I<sub>D</sub>/4)².

answer: Op-Amp. An operational amplifier is a high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with a very high input impedance and low output impedance, having two inputs (inverting − and non-inverting +) and one output. It was originally used for mathematical operations (add, subtract, integrate, differentiate) in analog computers. Output vo = AOL(v+ − v−); typical IC: 741 with supplies ±15 V.

Ideal Op-Amp characteristics: (1) Open-loop voltage gain AOL = ∞; (2) input resistance Ri = ∞ (input currents are zero); (3) output resistance Ro = 0; (4) bandwidth = ∞; (5) CMRR = ∞ (common-mode gain zero); (6) infinite slew rate; (7) zero input offset voltage and current (output zero when inputs are equal); (8) no drift of characteristics with temperature or supply voltage (PSRR = ∞); (9) infinite input voltage range and zero noise.
(Practical 741: A<sub>OL</sub> = 2 × 10<sup>5</sup>, R<sub>i</sub> = 2 MΩ, R<sub>o</sub> = 75 Ω, CMRR = 90 dB, SR = 0.5 V/μs.)

Virtual ground. Because AOL is very large, with negative feedback the output stays finite: v+ − v− = vo/AOL ≈ 0. Thus the two input terminals are at the same potential (virtual short). If the non-inverting terminal is grounded, the inverting terminal is at 0 V though it is not physically connected to ground – the virtual ground. Since Ri = ∞ no current flows into the op-amp, so the entire input current flows through the feedback resistor (used in deriving Av = −Rf/R1).

Slew rate. The maximum rate of change of the output voltage with time: SR = (dvo/dt)max in V/μs. It is caused by the finite charging current available to the internal compensation capacitor Cc (SR = Imax/Cc). If the signal demands a faster slope, the output is distorted (a sine wave becomes triangular).
Derivation of fmax. Let vo = Vm sin 2πft.
Step 1: dv<sub>o</sub>/dt = 2πfV<sub>m</sub> cos 2πft.
Step 2: maximum slope (at zero crossing) = 2πfV<sub>m</sub>.
Step 3: for distortion-free output this must not exceed the slew rate: 2πfV<sub>m</sub> ≤ SR.
Step 4: fmax = SR/(2πVm) (full-power bandwidth). Example: SR = 0.5 V/μs, Vm = 10 V → fmax = 0.5 × 106/(2π × 10) = 7.96 kHz.

Derivation. Step 1: v+ = 0, and with AOL → ∞, v− ≈ v+ = 0 (virtual ground).
Step 2: input current i<sub>1</sub> = (v<sub>i</sub> − 0)/R<sub>1</sub>.
Step 3: the op-amp draws no current (R<sub>i</sub> = ∞), so i<sub>1</sub> = i<sub>f</sub> = (0 − v<sub>o</sub>)/R<sub>f</sub>.
Step 4: vi/R1 = −vo/Rf → Av = vo/vi = −Rf/R1. The negative sign shows 180° phase inversion. Input resistance Rin = R1.

Design for Av = −3: Rf/R1 = 3. Choose R1 = 10 kΩ, then Rf = 30 kΩ (input impedance 10 kΩ); compensating resistor Rcomp = R1∥Rf = 7.5 kΩ at the non-inverting input is optional. For vi = 1 V, vo = −3 V.

(b) Non-inverting amplifier. The input vi is applied directly to the non-inverting terminal; the feedback network Rf (output to inverting input) and R1 (inverting input to ground) forms a voltage divider that returns a fraction β = R1/(R1 + Rf) of vo to the inverting terminal (negative feedback).
Operation: Any difference between v+ and v− is amplified by AOL and the output adjusts until the feedback voltage equals the input (virtual short): v− = v+ = vi.
Derivation. Voltage-divider: v− = voR1/(R1 + Rf) (no current into the op-amp).
Set v− = vi: vi = voR1/(R1 + Rf) → Av = vo/vi = 1 + Rf/R1.
Remarks: output is in phase with the input; gain is always ≥ 1; input resistance is very high (≈ Ri(1 + AOLβ)); with Rf = 0 (or R1 = ∞) it becomes a unity-gain voltage follower (buffer).

answer: (i) Summing (inverting adder) amplifier. Inputs v1, v2, v3 are applied through R1, R2, R3 to the inverting terminal; Rf is the feedback resistor, the non-inverting terminal is grounded.
Derivation. The inverting node is a virtual ground (0 V). KCL at this node (no current into the op-amp): i1 + i2 + i3 = if.
v<sub>1</sub>/R<sub>1</sub> + v<sub>2</sub>/R<sub>2</sub> + v<sub>3</sub>/R<sub>3</sub> = −v<sub>o</sub>/R<sub>f</sub>.

vo = −Rf(v1/R1 + v2/R2 + v3/R3). For R1 = R2 = R3 = R: vo = −(Rf/R)(v1 + v2 + v3); with Rf = R: vo = −(v1 + v2 + v3). Different resistor ratios give a weighted sum (e.g. D/A converter); a following inverter restores the sign. Inputs do not interact because of the virtual ground.

(ii) Difference amplifier (subtractor). v1 is applied to the inverting terminal through R1 with feedback Rf; v2 is applied to the non-inverting terminal through R2, with R3 from the non-inverting terminal to ground.
Derivation by superposition. (a) v2 = 0: inverting amplifier, vo1 = −(Rf/R1)v1.

(b) v<sub>1</sub> = 0: non-inverting amplifier with input v<sub>+</sub> = v<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>/(R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>3</sub>); v<sub>o2</sub> = (1 + R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>)·v<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>/(R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>3</sub>).
(c) Total: vo = −(Rf/R1)v1 + (1 + Rf/R1)(R3/(R2 + R3))v2.

For R2 = R1 and R3 = Rf the second coefficient becomes (R1 + Rf)/R1 × Rf/(R1 + Rf) = Rf/R1, hence vo = (Rf/R1)(v2 − v1); with all resistors equal, vo = v2 − v1. It amplifies the difference and rejects the common-mode signal (used in instrumentation amplifiers).

rubric.point: Definition of universal gates; NAND/NOR with truth tables and why universal
NOT, OR, AND using NOR only (circuit diagram/expression for each)

Proofs by Boolean algebra / De Morgan

answer: Universal gates. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any Boolean function (and hence any digital circuit) can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates; each can be used to realize the basic gates NOT, AND and OR. Truth tables: NAND Y = (AB)′ is 0 only when A = B = 1; NOR Y = (A + B)′ is 1 only when A = B = 0.

Reason: a NAND (or NOR) gate with its inputs tied gives NOT, and with an inverter after it gives AND (OR); since {AND, OR, NOT} is a functionally complete set, so are NAND and NOR. They are also cheaper and faster to fabricate in CMOS.
Realisation using NOR gates only:
NOT: tie both inputs: Y = (A + A)′ = A′.
OR: NOR followed by a NOT (a second NOR with inputs tied): Y = ((A + B)′)′ = A + B (2 NOR gates).
AND: invert each input using NOR-NOT, then NOR them: Y = (A′ + B′)′ = AB (De Morgan) (3 NOR gates).
Realisation using NAND gates only:
NOT: tie both inputs: Y = (A·A)′ = A′.
AND: NAND followed by a NAND-NOT: Y = ((AB)′)′ = AB (2 NAND gates).
OR: invert both inputs with NAND-NOTs, then NAND: Y = (A′·B′)′ = A + B (De Morgan) (3 NAND gates).
All equivalences follow from De Morgan's theorems (A + B)′ = A′B′ and (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
formulas: OR (NOR): A + B = ((A + B)′)′;  AND (NOR): AB = (A′ + B′)′

rubric.point: Statement of first theorem (A + B)′ = A′B′
Statement of second theorem (AB)′ = A′ + B′
Proof of both by truth table (4 rows, columns for A′, B′)

answer: First theorem: The complement of a sum equals the product of the complements: (A + B)′ = A′·B′ (a NOR gate equals an AND gate with inverted inputs).
Second theorem: The complement of a product equals the sum of the complements: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′ (a NAND gate equals an OR gate with inverted inputs).

Truth-table proof (A, B: 00, 01, 10, 11): (A + B)′ = 1, 0, 0, 0 and A′B′ = 1·1, 1·0, 0·1, 0·0 = 1, 0, 0, 0 – identical. (AB)′ = 1, 1, 1, 0 and A′ + B′ = 1, 1, 1, 0 – identical. Hence both theorems are proved.

Algebraic proof of the first theorem: Let X = A + B and Y = A′B′. If X′ = Y then X + Y = 1 and X·Y = 0. X + Y = A + B + A′B′ = (A + B + A′)(A + B + B′) = 1·1 = 1. XY = (A + B)A′B′ = AA′B′ + BA′B′ = 0 + 0 = 0. So Y is the complement of X: (A + B)′ = A′B′. The second theorem follows by duality (or by applying the first to A′ and B′).

Switching circuit: (A + B)′: two switches A and B in parallel form A + B; the complement is conducting only when both A and B are open, i.e. a series connection of normally-closed contacts A′ and B′ (A′B′). Likewise (AB)′: switches A and B in series form AB; the complement conducts if either A or B is open, i.e. parallel normally-closed contacts A′ + B′.
Use: converting AND-OR logic into NAND-NAND or NOR-NOR implementations.
